title: The graph-tool python library
abstract: Graph-tool is an efficient Python module for manipulation and statistical analysis of graphs (a.k.a. networks). Contrary to most other python modules with similar functionality, the core data structures and algorithms are implemented in C++, making extensive use of template metaprogramming, based heavily on the Boost Graph Library. This confers it a level of performance that is comparable (both in memory usage and computation time) to that of a pure C/C++ library.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

The graph-tool python library has clear scholarly uptake and functions as a software method anchor for graph and network analysis. It has accumulated 222 citations in OpenAlex, alongside 245 documented downstream reuse instances, showing sustained adoption across research outputs. The record also points to reach beyond a single niche, with citations appearing in high-visibility venues and across a broad mix of article, conference, and preprint literature.

Full narrative

The graph-tool python library, released through figshare in 2015 by Tiago P. Peixoto, was designed as an efficient Python module for graph manipulation and statistical network analysis, with core data structures and algorithms implemented in C++ for high performance. The impact record reflects that technical positioning: the software has been cited 222 times in OpenAlex and is also associated with 245 documented reuse instances, indicating that it has become part of the working infrastructure for subsequent scholarly research.

The citing landscape suggests durable and broad uptake rather than isolated reuse. Citations appear steadily across years, and the citing works span articles, conference papers, preprints, book chapters, dissertations, and software papers. The most visible citing venues include arXiv and bioRxiv, along with journals and proceedings such as Scientific Reports, PLoS ONE, Physical Review E, Physica A, and Journal of Complex Networks. This pattern is consistent with a tool that is used methodologically across computational, mathematical, and data-intensive fields.

The topical range of the citing literature is also wide. Network science and graph theory are prominent, but the library is also reused in work on opinion dynamics, graph neural networks, bioinformatics, brain connectivity, topic modeling, and data visualization. That spread suggests the software is not confined to one application area; rather, it serves as a general-purpose analytical backbone for studies that rely on network representation and inference.

The geography and institutional spread reinforce that interpretation. Citations are distributed across multiple countries, with the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, Australia, China, France, and Austria all represented among the citing record. Use appears concentrated in education-linked institutions, but it also extends into companies, government, nonprofit, and healthcare settings. Taken together, the record shows a mature and versatile software contribution with sustained academic visibility and practical reuse across several research communities.
